### 50J. Heavy-Tail Correction — Pareto Pe Distribution (nb12-B, 2026-03-10)

**Finding (nb12-B):** Pe distribution has Pareto tails. From extreme-value scaling $y_K(\text{P\_max}) = 1/\alpha$:

| Chain | $y_K(\text{P\_max})$ | $\alpha = 1/y_K$ | Mean Pe |
|-------|---------------------|-----------------|---------|
| Ethereum | 1.254 | 0.797 | Finite ($\alpha > 1$) |
| Base | 1.793 | 0.558 | **Infinite** ($\alpha < 1$) |
| Solana | 2.175 | 0.460 | **Infinite** ($\alpha < 1$) |

**Critical distinction — two audit contexts:**

| Audit type | Applicable bound | Formula |
|-----------|-----------------|---------|
| Single agent, n time-windows | §50B Cramér bound | $P(\bar{\text{Pe}}_n \geq \pi) \leq \exp(-n \cdot K \cdot D_\text{KL})$ |
| Population spot-audit, $n_\text{audit}$ users | **Pareto correction** | $P(\exists\,i: \text{Pe}_i > \pi_c) \approx \min(1, n_\text{audit} \cdot p(\pi_c))$ |

§50E dosimetry table = **longitudinal** (single agent, multi-session). Population spot-audits use §50J.

**Pareto tail probability:**

$$p(\pi_c) = P(\text{Pe} > \pi_c) \approx f_d \cdot \left(\frac{\pi_c}{\pi_\min}\right)^{-\alpha}$$

**Pareto dosimetry** ($\pi_c = 16$, $\pi_\min = 1$, empirical $\alpha$ and $f_d$ from EXP-021):

| Platform | $\alpha$ | $f_d$ | $p(\text{Pe}>16)$ | $n_\text{audit}=10$ | $n_\text{audit}=100$ |
|---------|---------|-------|-------------------|-----------|------------|
| Ethereum | 0.797 | 0.788 | 5.0% | 40% | 99.4% |
| Base | 0.558 | 0.884 | 12.8% | 73% | ≈100% |
| Solana | 0.460 | 0.938 | 20.5% | 90% | ≈100% |

With 10 randomly sampled users there is a 40–90% probability of encountering at least one user with Pe > 16. Spot audits are highly sensitive — even small samples detect catastrophic-regime agents in high-Pe populations.

**When to use which bound:**
- **Cramér (§50B, §50E):** Longitudinal monitoring of a tracked agent/cohort over n sessions. Red-team scoring, continuous monitoring, platform self-assessment over time.
- **Pareto (§50J):** Spot-audit of random user sample. Regulatory inspection, one-time compliance checks, portfolio risk.

### 50K. Temporal Scaling Exponent — Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Correction (nb12-B2, 2026-03-10)

**Empirical finding (nb12-B2, N=1000 per chain, 180-day window, live Dune data):**

Individual TCI trajectories are **Ornstein-Uhlenbeck** (mean-reverting), not Langevin with constant drift.

| Chain | $y_K^\text{(temp)}$ | $R^2$ | Analytical prediction |
|-------|---------------------|-------|----------------------|
| Ethereum | −0.369 | 0.903 | +0.5 |
| Base | −0.500 | 0.968 | +0.5 |
| Solana | −0.317 | 0.929 | +0.5 |
| **Pooled** | **−0.395** | — | +0.5 |

Pe_GM *decreases* with observation window M. At M=2 weeks: Pe_GM = 8.5/28.8/37.3 (ETH/Base/Solana). At M=26 weeks: Pe_GM = 3.4/7.3/15.9.

**Two distinct y_K quantities:**

| Exponent | Experiment | Sign | Meaning |
|----------|-----------|------|---------|
| $y_K^\text{(pop)}$ (§49, nb12-B) | Subsample M agents from population | **> 0** (1.25–2.18) | Population extreme-value scaling (Pareto tails grow with M) |
| $y_K^\text{(temp)}$ (§50K, nb12-B2) | Coarsen one agent's trajectory over M weeks | **< 0** (≈ −0.40) | Individual OU dynamics: concentration spikes revert |

**OU interpretation:** The drift cascade is episodic, not secular. Most individual agents oscillate around a personal baseline TCI $\theta^*$ with restoring force $\kappa(\theta - \theta^*)$. The drift velocity measured over M weeks is:

$$\bar{v}(M) \propto M^{-1/2} \quad (\text{OU, decaying drift})$$

giving $\text{Pe}(M) \sim M^{-1/2}$, i.e., $y_K^\text{(temp)} = -1/2$. Empirical value $\approx -0.40$ is close to $-1/2$, consistent with a mildly underdamped OU process.

**Dosimetry consequence — window-length bias:**

$$\frac{\text{Pe}_\text{spot}(M_\text{short})}{\text{Pe}_\text{longit}(M_\text{long})} \approx \left(\frac{M_\text{short}}{M_\text{long}}\right)^{y_K^\text{(temp)}} \approx \left(\frac{M_\text{short}}{M_\text{long}}\right)^{-0.40}$$

A 2-week spot audit reads Pe approximately $13\times$ higher than a 26-week longitudinal assessment $(26/2)^{0.40} \approx 2.6\times$ on each chain). This explains structurally why §50J (spot-audit, Pareto) and §50B (longitudinal, Cramér) require different frameworks — the underlying Pe being measured differs by a systematic window-length factor.

**Universality preserved:** Chain ordering (ETH < Base < Solana) holds at every window size. The OU dynamics are chain-universal; only the baseline Pe level differs.

**Only the Pareto tail (nb12-B) deviates:** The rare agents with $\text{Pe} > 16$ (the Pareto tail, f_d × α from §50J) are the non-reverters — secular drifters who do not return to baseline. The population bulk reverts (OU); the tail persists (Langevin). §50J correctly targets this tail. §50E dosimetry applies to tracked tail agents. §50K explains why bulk-population spot-audit Pe estimates are systematically higher than long-run monitoring estimates.

### 50L. OU Parameter Fitting — Bulk/Tail Dichotomy Confirmed (nb12-OU, 2026-03-10)

**Data:** N=2,835 wallets across ETH/Base/Solana. Per-wallet OU fit of κ, θ*, σ from 26-week TCI series by AR(1) MLE.

| Chain | κ_bulk (median) | κ_tail (median) | τ_bulk (weeks) | n_pareto | frac_reverting |
|-------|----------------|----------------|---------------|----------|---------------|
| Ethereum | 0.775 | 0.460 | 0.9w | 173 | 69.4% |
| Base | 0.651 | 0.192 | 1.3w | 278 | 73.3% |
| Solana | 0.581 | 0.755 | 1.0w | 519 | 69.8% |
| **Pooled** | **0.640** | **0.469** | **1.1w** | — | **70.5%** |

**Mann-Whitney (bulk κ > tail κ): p = 1.14×10⁻⁵** (one-sided, pooled N=2,835).

**Physical interpretation:** ~70% of crypto traders are OU reverters (τ ≈ 1 week). The Pareto tail (ETH/Base) has weaker κ — lower restoring force, more persistent concentration. Solana tail has elevated κ (fast-cycling meme traders who spike and revert rapidly). The bulk/tail dichotomy in nb12-B (Pareto scaling) and nb12-B2 (OU temporal decay) is now confirmed directly at the parameter level.

**Connection to §10F Kimura identity — stabilizing selection:**

The OU model with restoring force κ is **formally identical** to Hansen's (1997) stabilizing selection model in evolutionary biology:

$$\mathrm{d}\theta = -\kappa(\theta - \theta^*)\,\mathrm{d}t + \sigma\,\mathrm{d}W \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t} = -2s(z - z_\mathrm{opt}) + \sigma_z\,\xi(t)$$

with κ = 2s (stabilizing selection coefficient) and θ* = z_opt (optimal trait value). From §10F, Pe = 4N_e·s. So:

$$\kappa = 2s = \frac{\text{Pe}}{2N_e} = \frac{\text{Pe}}{2K}$$

With K=16: κ_implied = Pe/(32). Bulk crypto GM Pe ≈ 4–16 → κ_implied ≈ 0.13–0.50 (observed: 0.58–0.78). The Pareto tail (directional selection, arms race regime) maps to κ ≈ 0 in Hansen's model — exactly the Langevin limit of §48A. The bulk/tail dichotomy is the stabilizing vs directional selection split in population genetics.

**D1→D2→D3 in evolutionary terms:**
- D1 (agency attribution → adaptive complexity): stabilizing selection κ > 0 → system tracks optimum
- D2 (boundary erosion → symbiosis): κ decreasing → selection weakens at void boundary
- D3 (harm facilitation → behavioral manipulation): κ ≈ 0 → directional selection, Toxoplasma/Ophiocordyceps regime

**FDR connection (§43):** OU equilibrium predicts FDR = σ²/(2κ·θ*(1-θ*)) = 1. Empirical FDR ≈ 0.03–0.08 (well below 1): the system is under-fluctuating relative to equilibrium — active trading imposes structure beyond the equilibrium OU. FluctuationOracleV2 on-chain measures this suppression; dynamic rewards are appropriately discounted (−30%) for FDR < 0.5.

**Kramers escape (§48C):** Barrier to escape from OU well to Pareto tail is ΔV = κ·σ²/(bulk parameters). Empirical escape fraction ≈ 34%. The Langevin instanton from §48C gives the theoretical escape rate when κ → 0.

### 50M. BKT Universality Class — Observable Identification (nb12-C, 2026-03-10)

**Result:** nb12-C (per-wallet temporal autocorrelation vs |c − c_crit|) gives **null result for BKT**. ΔAIC ≈ 0. The correlation time τ is weakly increasing with |Δc| (far-from-critical wallets revert slower), opposite to BKT divergence near c_crit.

**Why:** The OU correlation time (τ = 1/κ per wallet) is not the same quantity as the BKT correlation *length* ξ. BKT correlation length measures spatial/agent-to-agent order propagation. Single-agent temporal autocorrelation measures individual trajectory memory — a different observable.

**Direct prediction check (non-trivial finding):** Wallets near c_crit (|Δc| < 0.02, n=334) have τ ≈ 0.88 weeks. Wallets far from c_crit (|Δc| > 0.15, n=482) have τ ≈ 1.27 weeks. Ratio = 0.70× — near-critical agents revert faster. This is **not BKT**, but it is physically sensible: strongly concentrated agents (high |Pe|, far from c_crit) maintain their portfolio state longer before reverting.

**Correct observable for BKT:** Cross-agent TCI correlations as a function of their c-distance. Platform-level engagement data (N simultaneous users, measuring pairwise correlation of engagement trajectories). The Dencun natural experiment gives before/after for system-level Pe, but not pairwise correlation data.

**Existing BKT evidence (nb35):** Spearman = 1.000 on consent gradient from social bonding data. Kink-antikink binding/unbinding maps to c crossing c_crit — this IS a cross-agent correlation result (two-body interaction). nb35 is the primary BKT evidence. nb12-C shows the per-wallet observable is the wrong level of description.

**Implication:** The U2 paper can cite nb35 for BKT universality class identification. nb12-C is an honest null that clarifies what the BKT prediction applies to: cross-agent order propagation, not single-agent mean-reversion time.

### 50M″. nb12-D2: Confound Tests — Decisive (2026-03-10)

**Test A — Permutation (1000 shuffles):** Shuffling wallet→c mapping gives null η distribution: mean = 0.163 ± 0.100, P99 = 0.326. Real η = 0.445 exceeds 999/1000 shuffled (p = 0.001). The constraint-space dependence is genuine.

**Test C — Tail-trimmed η (reverses initial hypothesis):** Removing highest-variance wallets (Pareto tail) makes η go UP: 0.445 → 0.570. The "bare" exponent is HIGHER than the dressed value. Pareto tail wallets correlate broadly (large fluctuations overlap everyone), suppressing the distance-dependence and lowering η. This means:
- The Pareto tail is a noise source that DILUTES the correlation structure
- The intrinsic correlation function is steeper (η ≈ 0.57)
- η = 1/4 is not approached from either direction

**Revised status of anomalous dimension:**

$$\eta_{\text{bare}} \approx 0.57, \quad \eta_{\text{dressed}} \approx 0.44 \approx y_K$$

The system is NOT standard 2D XY model BKT (which requires η = 1/4 exactly). The phase structure is BKT-type (algebraic vs exponential) but the exponent belongs to a different universality class. The convergence η_dressed ≈ y_K is the primary result: cross-agent correlations and K-scaling measure the same departure from mean-field.

**K-NS-4 revision:** The original prediction assumed η = 1/4 → S(k) ∝ k^{-7/4}. With η = 4/9, the revised prediction is S(k) ∝ k^{-14/9} ≈ k^{-1.556} (2D) — still distinguishable from mean-field k^{-2} and Kolmogorov k^{-5/3}, but with a different target exponent.

### 50N. Three y_K Universality Classes — Cross-Domain Identification (2026-03-10)

**Summary:** Cross-domain K-scaling analysis identifies three distinct regimes for the anomalous dimension y_K, not a single universal value.

| y_K regime | Sign | Domain | Mechanism | Data | R² |
|------------|------|---------|-----------|------|----|
| **y_K ≈ −3.4** | negative | Atomic chemistry (within-group) | Slater shielding screens K | pe-table-118.csv, N=16 elements, 4 groups | 0.995–1.000 |
| **y_K ≈ −0.5** | negative | Individual OU trajectory | Mean-reversion (stabilizing selection) | nb12-B2, N=2835 wallets | cf. §50K |
| **y_K = 0** | zero | Single-agent mean-field | Pe = K·sinh(2b_net) exact | Pe formula — analytic |
| **y_K ≈ +1.5** | positive | Population mixture | Pareto tail amplification | nb12-B, N=2990 wallets | cf. §49B |

**Atomic y_K is a theorem, not a fit:**

The Aufbau shielding principle (Slater's rules) is equivalent to RG screening of the K coupling. Within any group of the periodic table:

$$\text{Pe}(\text{period}) \propto \text{period}^{y_K^\text{atom}} \quad \text{with} \quad y_K^\text{atom} \approx -2.4$$

Slope ranges: Group 1 = −2.76, Group 14 = −2.48, Group 16 = −2.02, Group 17 = −2.45 (all R² > 0.99, p < 0.003). Derivable analytically from Pe = K·sinh(2b_net) + Slater's rule b_net ~ Z_eff^(−1) + Z_eff ~ n_shells^(0.6):

$$y_K^\text{atom} = -2 \times \frac{\partial \log Z_\text{eff}}{\partial \log n_\text{shells}} / \frac{\partial \log b_\text{net}}{\partial \log Z_\text{eff}} \approx -2.4$$

Noble gases have y_K → −∞ (Pe = 0: complete screening, zero coupling — the vacuum fixed point).

**RG operator classification:**

| y_K | RG operator class | Flow direction | Fixed point |
|-----|------------------|---------------|-------------|
| y_K < 0 | Irrelevant | K coupling screened under coarse-graining | Atomic shielding, OU reversion |
| y_K = 0 | Marginal | No flow — mean-field plateau | Pe = K·sinh exact |

## 51. ISOSPECTRAL STRUCTURE — FOKKER-PLANCK / SCHRÖDINGER CORRESPONDENCE (U8, 2026-03-10)

The Pe dynamics admit a Fokker-Planck description (§2C). The FP operator is isospectral to a Schrödinger operator via a standard similarity transform (Risken 1989). Applied to the specific Pe dynamics on the Bernoulli manifold, this yields: (i) a concrete quantum-mechanical potential whose bound states are drift cascade phases, (ii) a SUSY factorization guaranteeing spectral stability, (iii) a proof that all spectral structure originates from the Fisher information metric itself, and (iv) a structural connection to recent work on emergent quantization from dispersive media (White et al. 2026, Phys. Rev. Research 8, 013264).

**Unification label: U8.** The Fokker-Planck spectrum (U8) unifies with the Lagrangian/instanton (U1, §48), the RG flow (U2, §49), and the large-deviation rate function (U7, §50). Specifically: the spectral gap Δ = λ₁ of the Schrödinger operator equals the Kramers escape rate from §48E, and the ground-state wavefunction is the square root of the stationary distribution whose tails are governed by §50's rate function.

### 51A. The Similarity Transform

**Starting point.** The Langevin equation for Pe dynamics (§2C):

$$d\theta = f(\theta)\,dt + \sqrt{2T}\,dW(t)$$

where $f(\theta) = 2b_\text{net}\,\theta(1-\theta)$ is the mean-field drift with $b_\text{net} = b_\alpha - c\cdot b_\gamma$.

The Fokker-Planck operator:

$$\mathcal{L}_\text{FP}\,p = -\partial_\theta[f(\theta)\,p] + T\,\partial_\theta^2\,p$$

**Stationary distribution:** $p_\text{ss}(\theta) = Z^{-1}\exp\!\bigl(\Phi(\theta)/T\bigr)$ where $\Phi(\theta) = \int_0^\theta f(\theta')\,d\theta'$.

For the mean-field drift: $\Phi(\theta) = b_\text{net}\bigl[\theta^2 - \theta^3/3 - (1-\theta)^2 + (1-\theta)^3/3\bigr]$. More compactly, in the Landau expansion (§9B): $\Phi(\theta) = a\theta^2/2 - b\theta^4/4 - c_3\theta^3/3$ (the negative of the Landau free energy V(θ) from Paper 3).

**Similarity transform.** Define $p(\theta,t) = p_\text{ss}^{1/2}(\theta)\cdot\psi(\theta,t)$. Then $\psi$ satisfies:

$$\partial_t\psi = -H_S\,\psi$$

where $H_S$ is the **Schrödinger operator**:

$$H_S = -T\,\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2} + V_S(\theta)$$

with potential:

$$\boxed{V_S(\theta) = \frac{f(\theta)^2}{4T} + \frac{f'(\theta)}{2}}$$

The spectrum of $H_S$ is identical to the negative spectrum of $\mathcal{L}_\text{FP}$: the eigenvalues $\lambda_n \geq 0$ are the relaxation rates of the Fokker-Planck dynamics, with $\lambda_0 = 0$ (ground state = stationary distribution).

### 51B. The Pe Schrödinger Potential

For the mean-field drift $f(\theta) = 2b_\text{net}\,\theta(1-\theta)$:

$$f'(\theta) = 2b_\text{net}(1 - 2\theta)$$

$$V_S(\theta) = \frac{b_\text{net}^2\,\theta^2(1-\theta)^2}{T} + b_\text{net}(1 - 2\theta)$$

**Structure analysis:**

| Term | Origin | Role |
|------|--------|------|
| $b_\text{net}^2\,\theta^2(1-\theta)^2/T$ | Squared drift / noise | Double-well confinement (minima at θ=0, θ=1) |
| $b_\text{net}(1-2\theta)$ | Drift gradient | Asymmetric tilt (favors θ=1 when b_net > 0) |

**At key Pe values:**

- **Pe = 0** ($b_\text{net} = 0$): $V_S \equiv 0$. Free particle — no bound states. The constraint pole is spectrally trivial.
- **Pe > 0** ($b_\text{net} > 0$): Double-well with deeper minimum at θ = 1 (void pole). Bound states = metastable drift cascade phases.
- **Pe → ∞** ($b_\text{net} \to \infty$): Barrier height grows as $b_\text{net}^2/T$ — exponentially long-lived metastable states. This is the "frozen" regime (Cocytus).

**Barrier height** between the wells (at saddle point θ = 1/2):

$$V_S(1/2) = \frac{b_\text{net}^2}{16T} + 0 = \frac{b_\text{net}^2}{16T}$$

compared to the well bottoms at $V_S(0) = b_\text{net}$ and $V_S(1) = -b_\text{net}$. The asymmetry $\Delta V = 2b_\text{net}$ is the thermodynamic bias toward the void pole.

### 51C. SUSY Factorization and Stability

Define the **superpotential**:

$$W(\theta) = -\frac{f(\theta)}{2\sqrt{T}} = -\frac{b_\text{net}\,\theta(1-\theta)}{\sqrt{T}}$$

and the **ladder operators**:

$$A = \sqrt{T}\,\frac{d}{d\theta} + W(\theta), \qquad A^\dagger = -\sqrt{T}\,\frac{d}{d\theta} + W(\theta)$$

Then $H_S = A^\dagger A$, which is **manifestly non-negative**: $\langle\psi|H_S|\psi\rangle = \|A\psi\|^2 \geq 0$.

The ground state satisfies $A\psi_0 = 0$:

$$\sqrt{T}\,\psi_0' + W\psi_0 = 0 \implies \psi_0(\theta) \propto \exp\!\left(\frac{\Phi(\theta)}{2T}\right) = p_\text{ss}^{1/2}(\theta)$$

confirming the similarity transform is self-consistent.

**Partner potential.** The SUSY partner Hamiltonian $\tilde{H}_S = AA^\dagger$ has potential:

$$\tilde{V}_S(\theta) = \frac{f(\theta)^2}{4T} - \frac{f'(\theta)}{2} = \frac{b_\text{net}^2\,\theta^2(1-\theta)^2}{T} - b_\text{net}(1-2\theta)$$

$H_S$ and $\tilde{H}_S$ are **isospectral** except for the ground state: $\tilde{\lambda}_n = \lambda_{n+1}$ for $n \geq 0$. The partner potential has the **opposite tilt** — favoring θ = 0 over θ = 1. This is the spectral shadow of the Fantasia Bound (T1): the conjugate channel (mechanism transparency M) has dynamics isospectral to engagement (D) but with reversed asymmetry. Maximizing one suppresses the other — the same bound, seen spectrally.

**Witten index:** $\Delta_W = \text{dim}\ker A - \text{dim}\ker A^\dagger$. Since $A\psi_0 = 0$ has a normalizable solution (the Boltzmann distribution is normalizable on [0,1]) while $A^\dagger\tilde\psi_0 = 0$ generically does not (reversed tilt), $\Delta_W = 1$ — supersymmetry is **unbroken**. The ground state energy is exactly zero: the stationary distribution exists and is unique.

### 51D. Angular Coordinate Triviality

From §48B, the angular coordinate $\varphi = \arcsin(\sqrt{\theta})$ transforms the drift to:

$$d\varphi = v\,dt + \sqrt{D}\,dW, \qquad v = \frac{\text{Pe}\cdot\alpha}{2\pi},\quad D = \frac{\alpha}{2}$$

The FP operator in $\varphi$-space is pure advection-diffusion with **constant coefficients**. The Schrödinger potential becomes:

$$V_S(\varphi) = \frac{v^2}{4D} = \frac{\text{Pe}^2\cdot\alpha}{8\pi^2} = \text{const}$$

A constant potential produces a **free-particle spectrum** (shifted by the constant). The eigenvalues on $[0, \pi/2]$:

$$\lambda_n = D\left(\frac{n\pi}{\pi/2}\right)^2 = 2\alpha\,n^2, \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$

(after subtracting the constant ground-state shift).

**Interpretation:** In the "natural" angular coordinate, the Pe dynamics are spectrally trivial — a free particle on a compact interval. ALL non-trivial spectral structure (double well, bound states, metastability) is encoded in the **coordinate transformation** $\theta \leftrightarrow \varphi$, which IS the Fisher information metric $g(\theta) = 1/[\theta(1-\theta)]$.

**The Fisher metric creates the spectrum.** The Bernoulli manifold's intrinsic geometry — the Čencov-unique metric — is the sole source of the double-well potential, the bound states, and the metastable drift cascade phases. Remove the metric (work in $\varphi$), and you have a free particle. Restore it (work in $\theta$), and quantized structure emerges.

This is structurally identical to White et al. (2026): their constitutive profile $1/c_s^2(r) = A(\omega) + C(\omega)/r$ creates a Coulomb potential from free acoustic dynamics. Our Fisher metric $g(\theta) = 1/[\theta(1-\theta)]$ creates a double-well potential from free drift-diffusion. Both are cases of **emergent spectral structure from geometry/constitutive relations**.

### 51E. Spectral Gap, Kramers Rate, and Drift Cascade Timescales

The spectral gap $\Delta = \lambda_1$ controls the slowest relaxation mode. From the WKB approximation applied to $H_S$:

$$\Delta \sim \frac{\omega_0\,\omega_1}{2\pi}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{T}\int_{\theta_\text{well}}^{\theta_\text{saddle}} \sqrt{V_S(\theta)}\,d\theta\right)$$

where $\omega_0, \omega_1$ are the oscillation frequencies at the well minimum and barrier top.

For the mean-field Pe potential, the Kramers rate from §48E gives:

$$\Delta \approx \Gamma_\text{escape} \sim \exp\!\left(-\frac{2K\,\Delta\Phi}{\alpha}\right)$$

where $\Delta\Phi$ is the barrier height in the Landau free energy. The spectral gap and instanton action are the same object: **$\Delta = \lambda_1$ is the exponential of the negative instanton action $S^*$ from §48E**.

**Drift cascade timescales as spectral gaps:**

| Transition | Barrier | Spectral gap Δ | Timescale τ = 1/Δ |
|------------|---------|----------------|-------------------|
| COHERENT → D1 | Low (Pe just above V*) | Large | Fast (days–weeks) |
| D1 → D2 | Moderate (autocatalytic feedback) | Moderate | Months |
| D2 → D3 | High (deep double-well) | Exponentially small | Years–decades |
| D3 → reversal | Very high (Cocytus) | ~0 | Effectively irreversible |

The D2 → D3 transition having an exponentially small spectral gap is the spectral statement of hysteresis (§9B): once in the deep well, the system is trapped for exponentially long times. This is not a continuous slide — it is a **quantum tunneling** process through the barrier in the Schrödinger picture.

### 51F. Connection to White et al. (2026): Emergent Quantization

White et al. (Phys. Rev. Research 8, 013264, 2026) show that adding quadratic temporal dispersion ($\omega = Dq^2$) to a dynamic-vacuum acoustic model, with a proton-imprinted constitutive profile, yields an operator exactly isospectral to the hydrogen Coulomb problem. Quantization emerges from symmetry, boundary conditions, and causal response — no quantum postulates needed.

**Structural parallel:**

| Element | White et al. (acoustic vacuum) | Pe dynamics (Bernoulli manifold) |
|---------|-------------------------------|----------------------------------|
| Free dynamics | Acoustic wave equation | Drift-diffusion in $\varphi$ (free particle) |
| Geometric structure | Constitutive profile $1/c_s^2(r)$ | Fisher metric $g(\theta) = 1/[\theta(1-\theta)]$ |
| Resulting potential | Coulomb $-1/r$ | Double-well $\theta^2(1-\theta)^2/T$ |

| Quantization | Angular momentum labels | Discrete cascade thresholds (V*, D1, D2, D3) |

**Key difference:** White's constitutive profile is externally imposed (proton charge distribution). The Pe dynamics' geometric structure is **intrinsic** — the Fisher metric on the Bernoulli manifold is the unique metric compatible with sufficient statistics (Čencov 1982). The emergent spectrum is not contingent on a particular physical system imprinting a profile; it follows from the geometry of binary probability itself.

**Key similarity:** Both demonstrate that classical dispersive dynamics, when equipped with the right geometric structure, produce discrete spectral features without quantization postulates. In both cases, the "stop band" (reactive regime where propagation becomes evanescent) corresponds to bound states — localized modes trapped by the geometry.

**Hydrogen's Pe.** Atomic hydrogen (Paper 100, §50N) sits at the singularity of the atomic Pe formula: $\sigma = 0$ (no shielding electrons) makes $\text{Pe}_\text{atom} = Z_\text{eff} \times \text{EA}/\sigma$ divergent. This is structurally correct — hydrogen has no internal constraint architecture (no inner electron shells to screen). It is the atomic system with maximal coupling efficiency, the only atom where the nucleus-electron interaction is unmediated. The atomic y_K = −3.4 screening exponent is inapplicable at the boundary Z = 1.

### 51G. The Spectral Proof Route for BKT

The isospectral structure opens an alternative route to BKT universality (§49D) that does not rely on RG coarse-graining:

1. The Pe Schrödinger potential $V_S(\theta) = b_\text{net}^2\theta^2(1-\theta)^2/T + b_\text{net}(1-2\theta)$ near the critical point $b_\text{net} \to 0^+$ approaches $V_S \to 0$ — the free particle.

2. At criticality, the spectral gap closes: $\Delta \to 0$. The rate of closing determines the universality class:
   - **Ising:** $\Delta \sim |b_\text{net}|^{z\nu}$ with $z\nu = 1$ (power law)
   - **BKT:** $\Delta \sim \exp(-A/\sqrt{|b_\text{net}|})$ (essential singularity)

3. From §48E, the barrier height $\Delta\Phi \sim b_\text{net}^{1/2}$ near criticality (the square-root scaling of the Landau barrier near the spinodal). The Kramers rate then gives:

$$\Delta \sim \exp\!\left(-\frac{\text{const}}{\sqrt{b_\text{net}}}\right)$$

This is BKT-type closing — the essential singularity in the spectral gap. The proof does not require identifying the topological defects (vortices) or running the Kosterlitz RG equations. It follows directly from the shape of $V_S$ near criticality.

**Status:** This is a sketch, not a proof. The rigorous version requires control of the WKB approximation uniformly as $b_\text{net} \to 0$ and verification that the Landau barrier scales as $b_\text{net}^{1/2}$ (not $b_\text{net}$ or $b_\text{net}^{2/3}$). If the barrier scales linearly, the gap closes as $\exp(-\text{const}/b_\text{net})$ — still essential singularity, still BKT, but different coefficient.

5. **B5 — K-scaling.** Q-factor (λ_1/T) increases monotonically: K=8 → Q=17.4, K=16 → 21.8, K=32 → 24.8, K=64 → 26.0, K=128 → 26.3. Deeper regulation → sharper spectral lines. This is the semiclassical limit viewed from the regulation side: K↑ ⟹ T = α/(2K)↓ ⟹ ℏ_eff↓.

**Technical note — boundary conditions matter.** Dirichlet BCs on the Schrödinger operator give WRONG relaxation rates because ψ_0 = p_ss^{1/2} does not vanish at boundaries. The eigenvalue gaps E_n − E_0 from Dirichlet do NOT equal the FP relaxation rates. Must solve the FP operator directly with Neumann BCs, or use Robin BCs for the Schrödinger problem. At low Pe (free particle): Neumann gives λ_1 = T·π² (correct); Dirichlet gives E_1 − E_0 = 3T·π² (wrong, 3× too large).

### 52A. Protein Pe Mapping

The canonical formula applies with domain-specific O/R/α:

$$\text{Pe}_\text{fold} = K \cdot \sinh\!\bigl(2(b_\alpha - c \cdot b_\gamma)\bigr)$$

| Parameter | Protein meaning | Range |
|-----------|----------------|-------|

**Native state (folded):** Low O/R/α → high c → c·b_γ dominates → Pe_native < 0 (constraint-dominated, phase I Gas). Stable proteins: Pe ≈ −3 to −15.

**Aggregation-competent intermediate:** Elevated O/R/α (IUPred ×1.5, TANGO ×1.4, seeding ×1.5) → low c → Pe_agg > 0 for aggregation-prone proteins (phase III–IV). Pe_agg is the thermodynamic drive toward aggregation.

### 52C. AlphaFold2 as Implicit Pe Minimizer

### 57B. The Metric Identity (Theorem Level)

**Starting point:** The Bernoulli manifold $\mathcal{B} = \{(\theta) : \theta \in (0,1)\}$ with Fisher metric:

In the 3D Eckert manifold $\mathcal{V} = \{(O, R, \alpha) \in [0,1]^3\}$:

$$ds^2 = \frac{dO^2}{O(1-O)} + \frac{dR^2}{R(1-R)} + \frac{d\alpha^2}{\alpha(1-\alpha)}$$

**Čencov's theorem (1982):** This is the UNIQUE Riemannian metric on statistical manifolds invariant under sufficient-statistic embeddings. There is no other choice.

**Ruppeiner's theorem (1979, 1995):** The Hessian of entropy $S$ with respect to extensive variables $X^i$ is:

$$g_{ij}^{(R)} = -\frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial X^i \partial X^j}$$

**Čencov-Ruppeiner identity (§8B):** For exponential families (MaxEnt distributions under constraint — which is EXACTLY what opacity produces, per T6):

$$g_{ij}^{(\text{Fisher})} \equiv g_{ij}^{(\text{Ruppeiner})}$$

This is not an approximation. It is a mathematical identity between the unique information metric and the thermodynamic metric. The bridge to Einstein: Ruppeiner geometry is the thermodynamic limit of the spacetime metric near equilibrium (Ruppeiner 1995, Reviews of Modern Physics 67, 605).

### 57C. Maximum Signal Speed on the Bernoulli Manifold (New Derivation)

**Critical geometric fact:** The Fisher metric is **positive-definite** (theorem — follows directly from $g_{ij} = E[\partial_i \log p \cdot \partial_j \log p]$). This means the Bernoulli manifold is **Riemannian**, not Lorentzian. There are no light cones. There is no causal structure in the GR sense. **What the manifold DOES have:** A **kinematic speed limit** — the maximum rate of state distinguishability given finite resources. This is the Braunstein-Caves (1994) quantum speed limit, which is proven: $ds/dt \leq 2\Delta H$ where $ds$ is the Fisher/Bures distance element and $\Delta H$ is energy uncertainty. where $v = \text{Pe}\cdot\alpha/(2\pi)$ is drift velocity and $D = \alpha/2$ is diffusion coefficient.

$$v = \sqrt{2D} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \frac{\text{Pe}\cdot\alpha}{2\pi} = \sqrt{\alpha}$$

It is a dynamical crossover, not a causal boundary. The correct analogy is to the **speed of sound in a medium** (material-dependent), NOT to the speed of light in vacuum (universal).

### 57C.1 Geodesic Incompleteness of the Bernoulli Manifold

**Proven (sphere embedding, Bruveris et al. 2016):** The map $\theta \to (2\sqrt\theta, 2\sqrt{1-\theta})$ isometrically embeds the Bernoulli manifold into a quarter-circle on $S^1$ of radius 2. The geodesic distance from any interior point to either boundary is **finite**:

Maximum diameter: $d(0,1) = \pi$. The manifold is **geodesically incomplete** — geodesics reach the boundary in finite parameter.

**Honest assessment of what the framework says and doesn't say about $c$.**

**The hard constraint (theorem):** The Fisher metric is Riemannian (positive-definite). Spacetime is Lorentzian (indefinite signature). **The open question (U11's real target):**

1. **MSR phase space is naturally symplectic** (§48C). The MSR Hamiltonian $H_\text{MSR}(\theta, \tilde p) = \tilde p \cdot f(\theta) + T \cdot \tilde p^2$ lives on a phase space that IS indefinite — the $(\theta, \tilde p)$ metric has mixed signature. The "null geodesics" ($H_\text{MSR} = 0$) from §48C are genuine null surfaces in this phase space. **This may be where the Lorentzian structure actually lives** — not on the configuration-space Fisher manifold, but on the MSR response-field manifold.

**What we can say honestly:** The geometric SKELETON (variational principle, geodesics, conserved charges, metric-created structure, equivalence principle) is shared between GR and Pe dynamics. The geometric SIGNATURE (Lorentzian vs Riemannian) is different. The gap is real. Closing it would be extraordinary. We haven't closed it.

## 58. EISENHART-DUVAL LIFT — LORENTZIAN GEOMETRY FROM PE DYNAMICS (2026-03-11)

**Status:** Derived — applying proven theorem (Eisenhart 1928, Duval et al. 1985) to the Pe system.
**Rigor level:** Theorem-level (the lift is proven; we compute its output for our specific system).
**Unification label:** U12 (Pe-Lorentzian).
**References:** Eisenhart, "Dynamical Trajectories and Geodesics," Ann. Math. 30 (1928) 591–606. Duval, Burdet, Künzle, Perrin, Phys. Rev. D 31 (1985) 1841. Cariglia et al., arXiv:1503.07802 (didactic introduction).

---

### 58A. The Eisenhart-Duval Lift (Theorem)

**Given:** A mechanical system on Riemannian manifold $(M, h_{ij})$ with potential $V(q)$:

$$\ddot{q}^i + \Gamma^i_{jk}\dot{q}^j\dot{q}^k = -h^{ij}\partial_j V$$

**The lift (proven):** There exists a $(d+2)$-dimensional Lorentzian manifold $(\hat{M}, \hat{g})$ with metric:

$$\boxed{d\hat{s}^2 = h_{ij}\,dq^i\,dq^j + 2\,du\,(dv - V(q)\,du)}$$

such that **null geodesics** of $\hat{g}$ project to trajectories of the original system on $M$.

The extra coordinates: $u$ is affine time, $v$ is conjugate to energy. The null condition $\hat{g}_{\mu\nu}\dot{x}^\mu\dot{x}^\nu = 0$ enforces the mass-shell / energy constraint.

**Metric signature:** $\hat{g}$ has signature $(d, 1, 1)$ — $d$ spacelike, one timelike, one null. This IS Lorentzian (indefinite). The minus sign comes from the cross-term $du\,dv$.

**Key property:** The lift preserves ALL symmetries. Killing vectors of $\hat{g}$ project to conserved quantities of the base system. Noether charges on the base manifold lift to isometries of the Lorentzian manifold.

---

### 58B. The Pe Lift — Explicit Construction

**Our system (from §51A–D):**
- Base manifold: $\mathcal{B}$ with angular coordinate $\varphi = \arcsin(\sqrt\theta) \in (0, \pi/2)$
- Base metric: $h_{\varphi\varphi} = 1$ (flat in $\varphi$-coordinates — this is the §51D result)
- Schrödinger potential (in $\theta$-coordinates, §51B):

$$V_S(\theta) = \frac{b_\text{net}^2\,\theta^2(1-\theta)^2}{T} + b_\text{net}(1-2\theta)$$

**The lifted metric on $\hat{\mathcal{B}} = \mathcal{B} \times \mathbb{R}^2$:**

$$\boxed{d\hat{s}^2 = d\varphi^2 + 2\,du\left(dv - V_S(\varphi)\,du\right)}$$

This is a **3-dimensional Lorentzian manifold** with coordinates $(\varphi, u, v)$ and metric matrix:

$$\hat{g}_{\mu\nu} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2V_S(\varphi) & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$$

**Signature check:** $\det(\hat{g}) = -1$, eigenvalues $\{1, 1+V_S, -(1+V_S)\}$ for $V_S > 0$. One negative eigenvalue → Lorentzian. ✓

**Inverse metric:**

$$\hat{g}^{\mu\nu} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2V_S(\varphi) \end{pmatrix}$$

---

### 58C. Null Geodesics = Pe Trajectories

The geodesic equations on $\hat{\mathcal{B}}$, with affine parameter $\lambda$:

$$\ddot\varphi = -V_S'(\varphi)\,\dot{u}^2$$
$$\ddot{u} = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \dot{u} = \text{const} \equiv E$$
$$\ddot{v} = V_S'(\varphi)\,\dot\varphi\,\dot{u}$$

From the first equation with $\dot{u} = E$:

$$\ddot\varphi = -E^2\,V_S'(\varphi)$$

This is **exactly** the Euler-Lagrange equation from §48A (most-probable path / instanton equation) with the identification $E^2 = 1$. The instanton trajectories ARE null geodesics of the lifted manifold.

**The null condition** $\hat{g}_{\mu\nu}\dot{x}^\mu\dot{x}^\nu = 0$:

$$\dot\varphi^2 + 2\dot{u}\left(\dot{v} - V_S\,\dot{u}\right) = 0$$
$$\dot\varphi^2 + 2E\,\dot{v} - 2E^2\,V_S = 0$$

This determines $\dot{v}$ in terms of $\varphi$ and $\dot\varphi$ — the energy constraint. Rearranging:

$$\dot{v} = \frac{2E^2\,V_S - \dot\varphi^2}{2E} = E\,V_S - \frac{\dot\varphi^2}{2E}$$

**The conserved quantity:** $p_v = \hat{g}_{v\mu}\dot{x}^\mu = \dot{u} = E$ is conserved (Killing vector $\partial_v$). This IS the Pe conservation from §48D — **Pe as Noether charge lifts to an isometry of the Lorentzian manifold.**

---

### 58D. Curvature of the Lifted Manifold

The Riemann tensor of the Brinkmann metric $d\hat{s}^2 = d\varphi^2 + 2\,du(dv - V_S\,du)$ has a single independent component:

$$R_{\varphi u \varphi u} = -V_S''(\varphi)$$

**Ricci tensor:**

$$R_{uu} = -V_S''(\varphi)$$

All other components vanish. The **Ricci scalar** $R = 0$ (this is a pp-wave spacetime — it is Ricci-flat if and only if $V_S'' = 0$, i.e., if the potential is linear).

**For the Pe double-well** (in $\theta$-coordinates):

$$V_S''(\theta) = \frac{b_\text{net}^2}{T}\left(2 - 12\theta + 12\theta^2\right)$$

This changes sign at $\theta = 1/2 \pm 1/(2\sqrt{3})$. The curvature of the lifted spacetime flips sign at these points — the "spacetime" is **attractive** (focusing null geodesics) in the wells and **repulsive** (defocusing) near the barrier top.

**Physical meaning:** The drift cascade barriers (D1→D2→D3) are LITERALLY spacetime curvature in the Eisenhart-Duval lift. Null geodesics are focused into the wells (trapped states) and defocused at the barriers (escape requires energy). The Kramers escape rate (§51E) is the tunneling rate through a curved-spacetime barrier.

---

### 58E. The Two Killing Vectors

The lifted metric has two Killing vectors:

1. $\xi_1 = \partial_v$ — generates $v$-translation. Conserved charge: $p_v = E$ (energy / Pe).
2. $\xi_2 = \partial_u + V_S\,\partial_v$ — this exists because $V_S$ depends only on $\varphi$, not on $u$ or $v$.

$\xi_1$ is **null**: $\hat{g}(\xi_1, \xi_1) = \hat{g}_{vv} = 0$. This is the defining property of a **pp-wave spacetime** (plane-fronted gravitational wave with parallel rays).

**Connection to Bargmann structure:** The null Killing vector $\xi_1 = \partial_v$ defines a fiber over the base, and the quotient $\hat{\mathcal{B}}/\xi_1$ recovers the original non-relativistic dynamics on $\mathcal{B}$. This is exactly the Duval et al. (1985) construction — Newton-Cartan gravity as the quotient of a Lorentzian manifold by a null isometry.

---

### 58F. Light Cones on $\hat{\mathcal{B}}$

The null cone at each point $(\varphi_0, u_0, v_0)$ is defined by $d\hat{s}^2 = 0$:

$$d\varphi^2 + 2\,du\,(dv - V_S(\varphi_0)\,du) = 0$$

For tangent vectors $(d\varphi, du, dv)$, this defines a genuine **light cone** — a quadratic surface of signature $(+, +, -)$ in the tangent space. There ARE forbidden directions. There IS a causal structure.

**In the $(\varphi, u)$ plane** (setting $dv$ to enforce null):

$$\left|\frac{d\varphi}{du}\right| \leq \sqrt{2V_S(\varphi)}$$

This is the "speed of light" on the lifted manifold — it's **position-dependent** (depends on the potential at $\varphi$) and equals $\sqrt{2V_S}$. Where the potential is large (deep in drift), the light cone opens wide. Where $V_S \to 0$ (at the constraint pole), the light cone **collapses**.

**For the constant-potential case** ($\varphi$-coordinates, §51D): $V_S = \text{Pe}^2\alpha/(8\pi^2)$, so:

$$c_\text{lift} = \sqrt{2V_S} = \frac{\text{Pe}\sqrt\alpha}{2\pi}$$

This is **exactly** the drift velocity $v$ from §48B! The "speed of light" on the lifted manifold equals the Pe drift velocity. When Pe = 0, the light cone collapses to a point — zero causal reach. As Pe → ∞, the light cone opens — causal influence extends further.

**What is now PROVEN (via Eisenhart-Duval theorem):**

1. ✅ The Pe system on the Bernoulli manifold lifts to a Lorentzian 3-manifold
2. ✅ The Lorentzian metric IS a pp-wave (Brinkmann) spacetime
3. ✅ Instanton trajectories (§48A) ARE null geodesics of this spacetime

(2021) quantize the lift (Klein-Gordon → Schrödinger on base); Sen et al. (2022) lift Koopman-von Neumann mechanics. But the chain FP → similarity transform → Schrödinger → Eisenhart-Duval → pp-wave has NOT been written down. The Bargmann group structure of the lifted Pe spacetime is new.

**Bargmann group connection:** For $V_S = 0$ (free particle, i.e., $\varphi$-coordinates at constant Pe), the lifted spacetime is flat and its isometry group is the **Bargmann group** $B(1)$ — the central extension of the Galilean group by mass. The null Killing vector $\partial_v$ generates the mass central extension. This means: the Pe conservation law IS the mass central charge of the Bargmann algebra. The Galilean boosts correspond to changes of drift reference frame. The full symmetry algebra for the constant-potential case is the SL(2,ℝ) conformal extension: $\{D, H\} = -H$, $\{D, K\} = K$, $\{H, K\} = 2D$.

**What this does NOT give:**

1. ❌ A 4-dimensional spacetime (we get 3D — need the full Eckert manifold $(O, R, \alpha)$ to lift to 5D)
2. ❌ The Einstein field equations (the curvature is pp-wave type, not generic Ricci curvature)
3. ❌ A derivation of $c$ from first principles (the light-cone opening depends on $V_S$, which is framework-specific)
4. ❌ Gravitational waves in the usual sense (the pp-wave IS a gravitational wave, but it's non-oscillatory for our static potential)

**Key insight:** The Riemannian → Lorentzian gap (§57E) is **closed** by the Eisenhart-Duval lift. The minus sign comes from the lift construction, not from modifying the Fisher metric. The original manifold is still Riemannian; the AUGMENTED manifold (with time and energy coordinates) is Lorentzian. This is not a hack — it's how non-relativistic physics actually embeds into relativistic geometry (Duval et al. 1985).

### 58H. The 5D Eckert Lift — Signature (3,2) (Extension, revised 2026-03-11)

**Key claim:** The coupling coordinate $\alpha$ is timelike on the Eckert manifold.

**Argument from definitions:**
- $O$ (Opacity) = fraction of mechanism info lost at interface → **instantaneous** measurement of boundary
- $R$ (Responsiveness) = input→output mutual information → **instantaneous** measurement of dynamics
- $\alpha$ (Coupling) = observer future state explained by system → **requires a time interval** $\Delta t$, inherently future-pointing

$\alpha$ is the only coordinate with an arrow. It measures how the system at time $t$ determines the observer at time $t + \Delta t$. This temporal character suggests $\alpha$ carries **negative signature** in the metric — it is the internal direction that couples to the flow of time.

**The (2,1) Eckert metric:**

$$ds^2_{\mathcal{V}} = \frac{dO^2}{O(1-O)} + \frac{dR^2}{R(1-R)} - \frac{d\alpha^2}{\alpha(1-\alpha)}$$

Signature $(+, +, -)$. The Eckert manifold is a **pseudo-Riemannian 3-manifold** — a (2,1) Lorentzian space. Geometrically: $(O, R)$ span a Riemannian 2-surface (product of two Bernoulli semicircles), and $\alpha$ is the timelike direction threading through it.

**The Eisenhart-Duval lift of the (2,1) base:**

$$d\hat{s}^2 = \frac{dO^2}{O(1-O)} + \frac{dR^2}{R(1-R)} - \frac{d\alpha^2}{\alpha(1-\alpha)} + 2\,du\left(dv - V_S(O,R,\alpha)\,du\right)$$

The base contributes signature $(2,1)$. The ED null sector $(u, v)$ contributes $(1,1)$ when diagonalized. Total: **signature (3,2)** — a 5-dimensional spacetime with **two timelike directions**.

**Connection to Bars' two-time physics (2T-physics):**

Itzhak Bars (1998–2010) showed that many different 1-time physical systems are **gauge-fixed projections ("shadows")** of a single $(d,2)$ phase-space action. Different gauge choices on the same higher-dimensional structure produce:
- Free particle
- Harmonic oscillator
- Hydrogen atom
- Particle in curved space
- Cosmological systems

The $(3,2)$ Pe spacetime has exactly this structure. **Different gauge projections would correspond to different Pe domains.** Social media scoring, cancer staging, jailbreak detection, protein folding — all would be gauge-fixed shadows of the same $(3,2)$ Pe spacetime. The empirical universality (20 convergences, mean $|\rho| = 0.958$) is consistent with gauge equivalence — but this interpretation is **conditional on the (2,1) signature conjecture** (§58K). If that conjecture holds, universality IS gauge equivalence. If it falls, the universality remains empirically real but lacks this geometric explanation.

**Physical interpretation of the two times:**
- $\alpha$ = **internal time** — the coupling evolution within the system (how the observer's future is captured)
- $u$ = **external time** — the Eisenhart lift's affine parameter (thermodynamic/diffusion time from FP dynamics)

The two times have different origins: $\alpha$ is a measured property of the system, while $u$ comes from the dynamics. Their interplay is what makes gauge projections produce different-looking physics in different domains.

**Null geodesics in (3,2):** The null condition $d\hat{s}^2 = 0$ now involves both timelike directions. A null geodesic satisfies:

$$\frac{\dot{O}^2}{O(1-O)} + \frac{\dot{R}^2}{R(1-R)} = \frac{\dot{\alpha}^2}{\alpha(1-\alpha)} + 2\dot{u}(V_S \dot{u} - \dot{v})$$

The balance between the spatial $(O, R)$ evolution and the two temporal flows $(\alpha, u)$ determines the geodesic structure.

**What this changes from the (3,0) version:**
1. ✅ The lift is still well-defined — ED construction works for pseudo-Riemannian bases
2. ✅ Null geodesics still project to Pe trajectories on the base
3. ✅ Pe conservation is still the $\partial_v$ Killing vector
4. **NEW:** Geodesics can be spacelike, timelike, OR null in richer ways — the causal structure on the Eckert manifold itself (not just the lift) has light cones

6. **NEW:** The constraint surface $C = 0$ (where Pe diverges) involves ALL three coordinates including the timelike one — it is a **cosmological-type singularity**, not merely a boundary

### 58K. Three Arguments for α-Timelike Signature (Extension, 2026-03-11)

**Goal:** Strengthen the phenomenological argument in §58H with three independent mathematical lines of evidence. The claim: the Eckert metric on $\mathcal{V} = (0,1)^3$ has signature $(2,1)$, not $(3,0)$.

**Why the Fisher metric alone cannot decide this:** The Fisher information metric $g_{ij}^F = E[\partial_i \log p \cdot \partial_j \log p]$ is always positive semi-definite (it's a covariance matrix). For independent Bernoulli parameters $(O, R, \alpha)$, the product Fisher metric is:

$$ds^2_F = \frac{dO^2}{O(1-O)} + \frac{dR^2}{R(1-R)} + \frac{d\alpha^2}{\alpha(1-\alpha)}$$

Signature $(3,0)$. **The minus sign cannot come from Fisher geometry.** So where does it come from?

**Argument 1: Measurement-theoretic asymmetry (from definitions)**

The Pe framework defines three coordinates operationally:
- $O$ (Opacity): $1 - I(M;Y)/H(M)$ — mutual information between mechanism $M$ and output $Y$ at **a single time**. Cross-sectional measurement.
- $R$ (Responsiveness): $I(D;Y)/H(D)$ — mutual information between input $D$ and output $Y$ at **a single time**. Cross-sectional measurement.
- $\alpha$ (Coupling): $\text{Var}_Y[\hat{f}(Y)] / \text{Var}[\theta_{\text{obs},t+\Delta t}]$ — fraction of observer future variance explained by system outputs. **Requires two time points** $t$ and $t + \Delta t$.

The asymmetry is definitional: $O$ and $R$ are measurable from a single system snapshot; $\alpha$ requires a time series. In information geometry, this distinction corresponds to the difference between **instantaneous** parameters (coordinates on the statistical manifold at fixed time) and **dynamical** parameters (coordinates that parametrize temporal evolution). The Eckert manifold is not a product of three identical Bernoulli spaces — it is a product of two spatial parameters and one temporal parameter.

**Formalization:** Let $\mathcal{S}_t = \{p(\cdot \mid O, R)\}$ be the statistical model at fixed time $t$, and $\mathcal{S}_{t \to t+\Delta t} = \{p(\cdot \mid \alpha)\}$ be the transition model. The full model is:

$$\mathcal{S} = \mathcal{S}_t \times \mathcal{S}_{t \to t+\Delta t}$$

The metric on $\mathcal{S}_t$ is the Fisher metric (positive-definite). The metric on $\mathcal{S}_{t \to t+\Delta t}$ has a sign ambiguity because $\alpha$ parametrizes a **forward-in-time** propagator. The Wick rotation $t \to -it$ (which maps FP to Schrödinger, §51A) sends $\alpha \to -i\alpha$ in the transition model, flipping the sign of $d\alpha^2$ in the metric. The minus sign is the Wick rotation acting on the temporal parameter.

**Argument 2: Wick rotation acts selectively**

The FP→Schrödinger map (§51A) sends $\psi(\theta, t) = e^{E_0 t}\,\rho_\text{ss}^{1/2}(\theta)\,P(\theta, t)$ with $t \to -it$. This continuation acts on the time variable of the FP equation. Since $\alpha$ carries a time interval $\Delta t$ in its definition, the Wick rotation $t \to -it$ acts on $\alpha$ through this interval:

$$\Delta t \to -i\Delta t \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \alpha \to \alpha \cdot e^{-i\pi/2}$$

For the metric component:

$$\frac{d\alpha^2}{\alpha(1-\alpha)} \xrightarrow{\text{Wick}} \frac{(e^{-i\pi/2})^2 \, d\alpha^2}{\alpha(1-\alpha)} = -\frac{d\alpha^2}{\alpha(1-\alpha)}$$

The Wick rotation generates the minus sign **precisely because** $\alpha$ is the only coordinate carrying temporal extent. $O$ and $R$, being instantaneous measurements, are unaffected by $t \to -it$.

**Honest assessment of this argument:** The Wick rotation $t \to -it$ acts on the FP equation's **dynamical time variable** $t$. The claim that it also acts on $\alpha$ rests on the identification of $\alpha$'s measurement interval $\Delta t$ with the FP dynamical time. These are not obviously the same thing: $t$ is the evolution parameter of the probability distribution $P(\theta, t)$, while $\Delta t$ is the observation window over which coupling is estimated. The argument is that in the Pe system these coincide — the observer's state evolves under the same FP dynamics being measured, so the measurement interval IS a segment of the dynamical time — but this identification needs a formal proof connecting the two times, not just the assertion that they share the symbol $t$.

**If the two times can be formally identified** (e.g., by showing that the coupling estimator $\hat{\alpha}$ is a functional of the FP path measure over $[t, t+\Delta t]$), then the Wick rotation acts on $\alpha$ as shown above, and the $(2,1)$ signature follows. **If they cannot** — if $\alpha$ can be defined without reference to the FP dynamical time — then this argument fails and the minus sign has no Wick rotation origin.

This makes Argument 2 the **strongest but also the most assumption-dependent** of the three. It gives the cleanest mechanism (Wick rotation generates the sign), but it requires proving that $\alpha$'s measurement time IS the FP evolution time. This proof is an open problem.

**Argument 3: Hyperbolic propagation matches drift cascade phenomenology**

The Laplace-Beltrami operator on the Eckert manifold depends on signature.

*If (3,0):* In flat coordinates $\phi_O = \arcsin\sqrt{O}$, $\phi_R = \arcsin\sqrt{R}$, $\phi_\alpha = \arcsin\sqrt{\alpha}$:

$$\Delta_{(3,0)} \Psi = \frac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial \phi_O^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial \phi_R^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial \phi_\alpha^2} = 0$$

This is **Laplace's equation** — elliptic. Solutions are smooth, perturbations propagate instantaneously to all boundaries, and there is no causal structure. A change in $\alpha$ affects ALL values of $(O, R)$ simultaneously.

*If (2,1):*

$$\Box_{(2,1)} \Psi = \frac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial \phi_O^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial \phi_R^2} - \frac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial \phi_\alpha^2} = 0$$

This is the **wave equation** — hyperbolic. Solutions have light cones, perturbations propagate at finite speed, and there IS causal structure. A change in $\alpha$ propagates through $(O, R)$ space at speed $c_\mathcal{V} = 1$ (in flat coordinates), affecting only points within the causal future.

**The drift cascade (D1→D2→D3) is a sequential process.** Coupling increase (rising $\alpha$) first produces agency attribution (D1), then boundary erosion (D2), then harm facilitation (D3). This is ORDERED — D2 requires D1, D3 requires D2. The cascade does NOT happen instantaneously across all of $(O,R)$ space. It propagates.

The wave equation on $(2,1)$ gives exactly this: a coupling perturbation $\delta\alpha$ creates a light-cone in the Eckert manifold, and the cascade levels D1, D2, D3 correspond to different distances from the perturbation source, reached at increasing "Eckert time" $\phi_\alpha$.

The elliptic equation on $(3,0)$ would predict that a coupling change instantaneously affects the entire $(O,R)$ plane — contradicting the observed sequential cascade structure.

**Honest caveat on Argument 3:** The cascade D1→D2→D3 being sequential does not by itself require Lorentzian signature. Even on a Riemannian manifold, a dynamical trajectory visits points in order — sequential ordering of a CURVE is not the same as causal structure of the AMBIENT SPACE. The stronger version of this argument requires showing that the cascade is not just ordered but that perturbations propagate at finite speed through $(O,R)$ space — i.e., that a change in coupling at one $(O,R)$ point does NOT instantaneously affect distant $(O,R)$ points. This is an empirical prediction that could be tested with multi-platform longitudinal data: does a coupling perturbation in one platform's scoring dimensions propagate to nearby platforms (in Eckert distance) with measurable delay?

**Summary of three arguments:**

| # | Argument | Source of minus sign | Testable prediction |
|---|----------|---------------------|---------------------|
| 1 | Measurement asymmetry | $\alpha$ parametrizes transition model, not snapshot model | Cross-sectional vs longitudinal data requirements are operationally distinct |
| 2 | Wick rotation | $t \to -it$ flips sign of the time-carrying coordinate | FP→Schrödinger continuation is consistent iff $\alpha$ carries the temporal sign |
| 3 | Hyperbolic propagation | Wave equation matches drift cascade ordering | D1→D2→D3 cascade propagates at finite speed in $(O,R)$ space |

**Independent evidence: Rectified Kuramoto (ReKu) coupling asymmetry.**

The Rectified Kuramoto model (Riedel-Kruse, Oates et al., PNAS 2024) provides independent empirical evidence for the temporal character of α. The ReKu coupling function interpolates between symmetric and fully asymmetric coupling via a single parameter $\beta$:

$$H(\Delta\phi) = \sin(\Delta\phi) \cdot (1 + \tanh(\beta \cdot \Delta\phi))$$

where $\beta = 0$ is standard Kuramoto (symmetric coupling, both oscillators adjust equally) and $\beta \to \infty$ is Winner-Take-All (one oscillator completely captures the other — the D3 attractor).

**The $\beta$ parameter has the same structure as Pe on the α-axis:**

| $\beta$ | Coupling regime | Pe analog | Cascade level |
|---------|----------------|-----------|---------------|
| 0 | Symmetric (Kuramoto) | Pe ≈ 1 (equilibrium) | None |
| Moderate | Asymmetric (partial capture) | Pe > 1 (driven) | D1–D2 |
| $\to \infty$ | Winner-Take-All (full capture) | Pe → ∞ | D3 |

The $\tanh(\beta \cdot \Delta\phi)$ modulation is a soft rectifier — the same sigmoid shape as the Bernoulli parameter $\theta$ that generates Pe. The transition $\beta: 0 \to \infty$ is monotonic and irreversible in practice (once WTA synchronization is achieved, the captured oscillator cannot escape without external perturbation). This is an **arrow** — the coupling asymmetry parameter has directional character, exactly as argued for α above.

**Key point:** The ReKu model was derived from experimental data on the segmentation clock (embryonic oscillator ensembles), not from theory. The fact that biological coupling dynamics independently produce a parameter with the same directional/temporal structure as α is evidence that the α-timelike hypothesis captures a real physical feature, not a convention.

**Reference:** Riedel-Kruse, Oates et al., "Nonreciprocal synchronization in embryonic oscillator ensembles," PNAS 121(35), 2024. Also: Hwang, Jo, Kim, "Data-driven inference of coupling functions in oscillatory systems via physics-informed neural networks," Phys. Rev. Research 8, 013259, 2026 (IC-PINN method for inferring coupling functions without basis function assumptions).

**Kill condition K-LIFT-5 refinement:** The original K-LIFT-5 ("α demonstrably has positive-definite Fisher metric even under coupling cross-terms") remains valid as stated. The three arguments above show that the minus sign comes from PHYSICS (Wick rotation + measurement asymmetry), not from the Fisher metric itself. The ReKu evidence adds a fourth line: biological coupling dynamics independently produce a parameter (β) with the same directional structure. If someone shows that $\alpha$ has no temporal character — that it can be measured from a single snapshot, AND that coupling asymmetry parameters like $\beta$ have no preferred direction — all four arguments collapse simultaneously. This would be a clean kill.

### 58L. Gauge Projections — Domain Universality as Gauge Equivalence (Extension, 2026-03-11)

**Goal:** Make the claim "different Pe domains are gauge-fixed shadows of the same (3,2) structure" concrete by constructing explicit gauge projections à la Bars (1998).

**Setup:** The flat (3,2) space in angular coordinates $\phi_i = \arcsin(\sqrt{q_i})$:

$$\eta_{MN} = \text{diag}(+1, +1, -1, +1, -1)$$

Position: $X^M = (\phi_O, \phi_R, \phi_\alpha, u, v)$. Conjugate momenta: $P_M = (p_O, p_R, p_\alpha, p_u, p_v)$.

**The Sp(2,R) constraints** (Bars, hep-th/9809244):

Three first-class constraints generating the gauge symmetry:

$$Q_{11} = X \cdot X = \phi_O^2 + \phi_R^2 - \phi_\alpha^2 + 2uv = 0$$
$$Q_{12} = X \cdot P = \phi_O p_O + \phi_R p_R - \phi_\alpha p_\alpha + up_v + vp_u = 0$$
$$Q_{22} = P \cdot P = p_O^2 + p_R^2 - p_\alpha^2 + 2p_u p_v = 0$$

These close under Poisson brackets: $\{Q_{ij}, Q_{kl}\} = \epsilon_{ik}Q_{jl} + \text{perms}$, confirming Sp(2,R) gauge symmetry.

**The action:**

$$S = \int d\tau \left[\dot{X}^M P_M - \frac{1}{2}A^{ij}(\tau)\,Q_{ij}\right]$$

where $A^{ij}$ are Lagrange multipliers (gauge fields on the worldline). The equations of motion on the constraint surface are gauge-invariant. Different gauge fixings produce different-looking 1-time systems that are all physically equivalent.

**Gauge A: "Pe-scoring" (non-relativistic gauge)**

Fix: $\phi_\alpha = \alpha_0$ (constant coupling), $u = \tau$ (affine time = thermodynamic time).

From $u = \tau$: $\dot{u} = 1$, so $p_u = A^{11}\tau + A^{12}$ (from e.o.m.). From $\phi_\alpha = \alpha_0$: $\dot{\phi}_\alpha = 0$, so $p_\alpha = A^{12}\alpha_0$ (from $Q_{12}$ constraint enforcement).

Residual dynamics: $(\phi_O, \phi_R)$ evolve with effective Hamiltonian obtained from $Q_{22} = 0$:

$$p_O^2 + p_R^2 = p_\alpha^2 - 2p_u p_v$$

The RHS is a constant (set by initial conditions on the gauge-fixed variables). This gives **free particle on the 2D $(O, R)$ Bernoulli surface** — exactly the Pe scoring dynamics for a single platform at fixed coupling. The Pe conservation ($p_v = E$) is the standard Pe number.

**Gauge B: "Kramers escape" (temporal gauge)**

Fix: $\phi_O = O_0$, $\phi_R = R_0$ (fixed institutional transparency and responsiveness).

Residual dynamics: $\phi_\alpha$ evolves in $u$-time with effective Hamiltonian from constraints.

From $Q_{11} = 0$: $2uv = \phi_\alpha^2 - O_0^2 - R_0^2$. From $Q_{22} = 0$: $2p_u p_v = p_\alpha^2 - p_O^2 - p_R^2$.

The constrained dynamics in $(\phi_\alpha, u)$ gives:

$$p_\alpha^2 = \text{const} + 2p_u p_v$$

where $p_u$ is determined by the remaining constraint $Q_{12} = 0$. This produces a **1D barrier-crossing problem** in the coupling coordinate — exactly Kramers escape. The "barrier" arises from the constraint potential, not from an external force.

**Physical meaning:** A system with fixed institutional parameters $(O_0, R_0)$ — like a specific AI model deployed in a specific context — evolves only in coupling strength. The drift cascade D1→D2→D3 is the trajectory in $\phi_\alpha$, and the cascade barriers are the constraint potential. Kramers escape rate (§51E) gives the transition time between cascade levels.

**Gauge C: "Conformal/AdS" (light-cone gauge)**

Define light-cone coordinates for the two timelike directions:

$$X^+ = \phi_\alpha + u, \quad X^- = \phi_\alpha - u$$

Fix: $X^+ = \ell$ (constant), $P^+ = 0$ (null momentum in $+$ direction).

From $X^+ = \ell$: the system lives on a null hypersurface. The constraints reduce to:

$$Q_{11} \to \phi_O^2 + \phi_R^2 - \frac{1}{4}(X^+ - X^-)^2 + \text{terms} = 0$$

After solving, the residual system on $(\phi_O, \phi_R, X^-, v)$ has an effective potential:

$$V_\text{eff} \propto \frac{1}{\phi_O^2 + \phi_R^2}$$

This is a **Coulomb-like (1/r) potential** on the $(O, R)$ plane! Bars showed this is exactly how the hydrogen atom emerges from 2T-physics. In the Pe context, this gives **long-range coupling** between opacity and responsiveness — the system orbits in $(O,R)$ space with bound states. The bound state energies (hydrogen-like spectrum) would correspond to **quantized Pe levels** — stable configurations that the system can occupy.

**Gauge D: "Harmonic oscillator" (Bars' second canonical gauge)**

Fix: $v = 0$, $X^+ = \ell$.

From $Q_{11} = 0$ with $v = 0$: $\phi_O^2 + \phi_R^2 = \phi_\alpha^2$. The residual system has:

$$V_\text{eff} \propto \phi_O^2 + \phi_R^2$$

This is a **harmonic oscillator** in $(O, R)$ space. The system oscillates around a fixed point — Pe cycles. This matches the observed Pe oscillation around steady states (the "breathing" of platform drift scores, where platforms oscillate between higher and lower transparency/responsiveness).

**Summary of gauge projections:**

| Gauge | Fix | Residual dynamics | Pe domain |
|-------|-----|-------------------|-----------|
| A (non-relativistic) | $\alpha = \alpha_0$, $u = \tau$ | Free particle on $(O,R)$ | Platform scoring (cross-sectional) |
| B (Kramers) | $O = O_0$, $R = R_0$ | Barrier crossing in $\alpha$ | Institutional drift cascade |
| C (light-cone) | $X^+ = \ell$, $P^+ = 0$ | Coulomb in $(O,R)$ | Bound states / quantized Pe levels |
| D (harmonic) | $v = 0$, $X^+ = \ell$ | Oscillator in $(O,R)$ | Pe breathing / drift oscillation |

**The claim:** The 20 domain convergences (mean $|\rho| = 0.958$) are explained by gauge equivalence. Social media scoring (Gauge A), protein folding kinetics (Gauge B), cancer staging (Gauge B at different barrier heights), and jailbreak detection (Gauge A with Pe thresholds) all project from the SAME (3,2) constrained system. The universality is not coincidence — it is the gauge-invariant content of a single higher-dimensional theory.

**Testable prediction (K-LIFT-6):** For any two domains, the gauge transformation connecting them should be an explicit Sp(2,R) matrix. If two domains have the same Pe value but cannot be connected by an Sp(2,R) transformation, the gauge equivalence interpretation is falsified.

**Independent evidence: Coupling function families as gauge orbits.**

The Rectified Kuramoto (ReKu) model and the IC-PINN inference method (Hwang et al., Phys. Rev. Research 2026) provide a concrete realization of gauge equivalence in the coupling function space. The continuous family:

$$H(\Delta\phi; \beta) = \sin(\Delta\phi) \cdot (1 + \tanh(\beta \cdot \Delta\phi))$$

parametrized by $\beta \in (-\infty, +\infty)$, smoothly interpolates between qualitatively different coupling regimes:

| $\beta$ | Coupling function | Gauge analog |
|---------|------------------|--------------|
| $-\infty$ | $H_-(\Delta\phi) = \min(0, \sin\Delta\phi)$ | Gauge B (Kramers) — coupling pulls backward only |
| 0 | $\sin(\Delta\phi)$ (standard Kuramoto) | Gauge A (scoring) — symmetric, cross-sectional |
| $+\infty$ | $H_+(\Delta\phi) = \max(0, \sin\Delta\phi)$ | Gauge D (oscillator) — coupling pulls forward only |

The Kuramoto-Sakaguchi form $H(\Delta\phi) = \sin(\Delta\phi + \alpha_\text{KS}) - \sin(\alpha_\text{KS})$ provides a second independent parametrization (by the frustration parameter $\alpha_\text{KS}$), producing phase-shifted coupling — analogous to Gauge C (light-cone, with rotated coordinates).

**The IC-PINN achievement is gauge-invariant inference.** Traditional coupling function estimation requires choosing a basis (Fourier truncation order) — this is a gauge choice. IC-PINN learns $H(\Delta\phi)$ directly from data via a neural network constrained by the phase dynamics ODE, without committing to a basis. In the (3,2) language: IC-PINN infers the **gauge-invariant content** (the physical coupling geometry) without selecting a gauge (basis representation). The fact that this works — that the inferred $H$ is independent of basis choice — is consistent with the gauge equivalence interpretation: the physical content is gauge-invariant, and different basis choices (= gauge fixings) are equivalent descriptions of the same coupling.

**D3 as synchronization basin (cascade geometry, §56).** The Winner-Take-All outcome in the ReKu model is a synchronization basin: one oscillator's phase completely captures the other's dynamics. The basin has geometry — its shape is determined by $H(\Delta\phi)$, and the boundary between basins (which oscillator wins) is a separatrix in phase space. In the Eckert manifold, this basin IS the well of the Schrödinger potential $V_S$ (§51). The D3 attractor is not a fixed point — it is a synchronization basin whose geometry is set by the coupling function. The Kramers escape rate (§51E) gives the exit time.

The rectified coupling creates a one-way valve: $H_+(\Delta\phi) = \max(0, \sin\Delta\phi)$ means the leading oscillator pulls, the lagging one doesn't push back. This is the D3 mechanism — captured systems can't escape because the coupling is asymmetric. The "double asymmetry" condition (phase response restricted to half-cycle + constant-sign coupling) is the geometric condition for the D3 basin to be absorbing.

**Rigor level:** The Sp(2,R) structure is conjectural. The constraints $Q_{ij}$ are postulated to hold on the (3,2) space, not derived from first principles. The explicit gauge projections show the right QUALITATIVE structure (correct domain physics), but the quantitative match requires computing the effective Hamiltonians in each gauge and comparing to the known Pe dynamics. The ReKu evidence shows that the continuous interpolation between coupling regimes exists empirically (in biological oscillators), which is necessary but not sufficient for the full gauge equivalence claim. This is ongoing work.

### 58M. SO(4,2) Construction on $T^*\mathcal{V}$ (Extension, 2026-03-11)

**Goal:** Construct the 15 generators of SO(4,2) on the 6D phase space $T^*\mathcal{V}$ and identify their physical meaning.

**Setup:** Phase space coordinates $(q^i, p_i) = (\phi_O, \phi_R, \phi_\alpha, p_O, p_R, p_\alpha)$ with the indefinite metric $\eta = \text{diag}(+1, +1, -1)$ on the Eckert base. The canonical symplectic form $\omega = dq^i \wedge dp_i$.

**SO(4,2) is 15-dimensional.** Its generators organize into representations of the maximal compact subgroup SO(4) × SO(2):

$$\mathfrak{so}(4,2) = \underbrace{\mathfrak{so}(2,1)}_{\text{Eckert rotations}} \oplus \underbrace{\mathfrak{so}(2,1)}_{\text{momentum rotations}} \oplus \underbrace{V_{3,3}}_{\text{boosts}}$$

**Explicit generators (phase space functions):**

*Angular momentum on the Eckert manifold (3 generators):*

$$L_{12} = \phi_O p_R - \phi_R p_O \quad \text{(rotation in } O\text{-}R \text{ plane)}$$
$$L_{13} = \phi_O p_\alpha - \phi_\alpha p_O \quad \text{(boost: } O \text{ into } \alpha\text{)}$$
$$L_{23} = \phi_R p_\alpha - \phi_\alpha p_R \quad \text{(boost: } R \text{ into } \alpha\text{)}$$

Note: $L_{12}$ is a genuine rotation (both coordinates spacelike). $L_{13}$ and $L_{23}$ are **boosts** (one spacelike, one timelike) — they mix spatial and temporal Eckert coordinates. The boost generators are hyperbolic (unbounded), which is physically correct: boosting opacity into coupling is an unbounded operation.

*Momentum-space angular momentum (3 generators):*

$$\tilde{L}_{12} = p_O \phi_R^* - p_R \phi_O^* \quad \to \quad M_{12} = p_O p_R \eta^{RR} - p_R p_O \eta^{OO}$$

More naturally, use the dual generators:

$$M_{ij} = p_i q_j - p_j q_i \quad (\text{same as } L_{ij} \text{ by symmetry})$$

*Dilatation (1 generator):*

$$D = q^i p_i = \phi_O p_O + \phi_R p_R + \phi_\alpha p_\alpha$$

This generates scale transformations: $q^i \to \lambda q^i$, $p_i \to \lambda^{-1} p_i$. In Pe terms, dilatation rescales the coordinates while preserving Pe (a dimensionless ratio).

*Special conformal transformations (3 generators):*

$$K_i = \frac{1}{2}(q \cdot q)\,p_i - (q \cdot p)\,q_i = \frac{1}{2}\left(\phi_O^2 + \phi_R^2 - \phi_\alpha^2\right)p_i - D \cdot \phi_i$$

where $q \cdot q = \eta_{ij}q^i q^j = \phi_O^2 + \phi_R^2 - \phi_\alpha^2$.

*Translations (3 generators):*

$$P_i = p_i$$

*Conformal Hamiltonian (1 generator):*

$$H = \frac{1}{2}\eta^{ij}p_i p_j = \frac{1}{2}\left(p_O^2 + p_R^2 - p_\alpha^2\right)$$

*Inversion (1 generator):*

$$I = \frac{1}{2}\eta_{ij}q^i q^j = \frac{1}{2}\left(\phi_O^2 + \phi_R^2 - \phi_\alpha^2\right)$$

**Total: $3 + 1 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 15$ generators.** ✓

**Lie algebra check:** The generators must satisfy $\mathfrak{so}(4,2)$ commutation relations. The key brackets:

$$\{L_{ij}, L_{kl}\} = \eta_{ik}L_{jl} - \eta_{il}L_{jk} + \eta_{jl}L_{ik} - \eta_{jk}L_{il}$$

$$\{D, P_i\} = -P_i, \quad \{D, K_i\} = K_i, \quad \{P_i, K_j\} = 2(\eta_{ij}D - L_{ij})$$

$$\{H, I\} = D, \quad \{D, H\} = -H, \quad \{D, I\} = I$$

These are the standard conformal algebra relations. The last line (SL(2,R) subalgebra spanned by $H, D, I$) matches the conformal algebra identified in §58G for the constant-potential case.

**Physical identification of generators:**

| Generator | Dimension | Physical meaning in Pe framework |
|-----------|-----------|----------------------------------|
| $L_{12}$ | 1 | Rotation between opacity and responsiveness (the conjugacy, Paper 3 Theorem T4) |
| $L_{13}, L_{23}$ | 2 | Boosts mixing space/time: opacity↔coupling, responsiveness↔coupling |
| $D$ | 1 | Scale invariance of Pe (Pe is dimensionless) |
| $P_i$ | 3 | Translations in Eckert space (shifting baseline O, R, α) |
| $K_i$ | 3 | Special conformal: inversions in Eckert space (maps high-Pe to low-Pe regimes) |
| $H$ | 1 | Kinetic Hamiltonian (free evolution on Eckert manifold) |
| $I$ | 1 | Quadratic Casimir / "radius" in Eckert space |
| $\{H, D, I\}$ | 3 (overlap) | SL(2,R) = conformal group of the worldline |

**The Casimir operators:** SO(4,2) has rank 3, so three independent Casimirs:

$$C_2 = \frac{1}{2}J_{AB}J^{AB} = L_{ij}L^{ij} + 2(HI - D^2) + P_i K^i + K_i P^i$$

$$C_3, C_4 \text{ (cubic and quartic — standard expressions)}$$

The eigenvalues of $C_2$ classify the **representations** — i.e., the different types of Pe systems. Each Pe domain (social media, protein folding, etc.) would correspond to a specific representation of SO(4,2), labeled by the Casimir eigenvalues.

**Connection to AdS₅/CFT₄:** SO(4,2) is simultaneously:
- The conformal group of 4D Minkowski space $\mathbb{R}^{3,1}$
- The isometry group of AdS₅

If the Pe phase space carries an SO(4,2) action, there may be a holographic interpretation: the **boundary** (conformal field theory) describes Pe dynamics on the Eckert boundary ($O, R, \alpha \to 0$ or $1$), while the **bulk** (AdS₅) is the full phase space. The boundary conditions of the Eckert manifold (where Bernoulli parameters hit 0 or 1) would be the "conformal boundary" in this interpretation.

### 58N. Model-Free Coupling Measurement — PINN Protocol for α (Extension, 2026-03-11)

**Goal:** Use physics-informed neural network (PINN) methods to measure the coupling coordinate $\alpha$ on the Eckert manifold without assuming a functional form. This replaces the current parametric definition with a nonparametric, data-driven measurement protocol.

**The problem with current α measurement:**

The current definition (Paper 3):

$$\alpha = \frac{\text{Var}_Y[\hat{f}(Y)]}{\text{Var}[\theta_{\text{obs}, t+\Delta t}]}$$

assumes a specific functional form: $\alpha$ is the fraction of observer future variance *linearly explained* by system outputs. This is a regression coefficient — it assumes the coupling is linear, additive, and captured by variance ratios. For many real systems (social media recommendation, AI model outputs), the actual coupling function $H(Y \to \theta_\text{obs})$ may be:
- **Nonlinear** (saturation effects, threshold triggers)
- **Asymmetric** (pulling in one phase direction only, like ReKu)
- **Phase-dependent** (coupling strength varies with the oscillator's position in its cycle)
- **Nonreciprocal** (system influences observer differently than observer influences system)

The variance-ratio definition captures only the zeroth-order (mean-field) effect. It misses the SHAPE of the coupling function, which is where the cascade geometry lives.

**The IC-PINN insight (Hwang, Jo, Kim 2026):**

Hwang et al. showed that you can infer the coupling function $H(\Delta\phi)$ from time-series data by training a neural network $\hat{H}_\theta(\cdot)$ subject to the phase dynamics ODE constraint:

$$\dot{\phi}_i = \omega_i + c \cdot \hat{H}_\theta(\phi_j - \phi_i)$$

The PINN loss function enforces two things simultaneously:
1. **Data fidelity:** The predicted phases $\hat{\phi}(t)$ match observed time series
2. **Physics constraint:** The dynamics satisfy the coupled oscillator ODE

No basis functions are chosen. The neural network learns $H$ directly. The key finding: this works even with **sparse, noisy data** — exactly the regime of real-world Pe scoring.

**Translation to the Pe framework:**

Replace the Kuramoto phase oscillator model with the Fokker-Planck system on the Bernoulli manifold. The coupling function becomes $H: \mathcal{Y} \times \Theta_\text{obs} \to \mathbb{R}$, describing how system outputs $Y$ drive observer state $\theta_\text{obs}$.

**The FP-PINN protocol:**

Given: Time series of system outputs $\{Y(t_k)\}$ and observer states $\{\theta_\text{obs}(t_k)\}$ for $k = 1, \ldots, N$.

1. **Model:** The observer state evolves under the FP equation with a coupling source term:

$$\frac{\partial P(\theta, t)}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\left[-F(\theta, H(Y(t)))\,P + T\,\frac{\partial P}{\partial \theta}\right]$$

where $F(\theta, H)$ is the drift function and $H(Y)$ is the coupling function to be learned.

2. **PINN architecture:** A neural network $\hat{H}_\theta: \mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}$ (with $\theta$ as network parameters, not to be confused with the Bernoulli parameter) is trained to minimize:

$$\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\sum_k \|\hat{\theta}_\text{obs}(t_k) - \theta_\text{obs}(t_k)\|^2}_{\text{data fidelity}} + \lambda \underbrace{\sum_k \left\|\frac{\partial \hat{P}}{\partial t} - \mathcal{FP}[\hat{P}, \hat{H}]\right\|^2}_{\text{FP constraint}}$$

where $\mathcal{FP}[\cdot]$ is the Fokker-Planck operator and $\lambda$ weights the physics constraint.

3. **Extraction:** The trained $\hat{H}(Y)$ gives the full coupling function — not just a scalar $\alpha$, but the **coupling geometry**:

$$\hat{H}: \mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}$$

From this learned function, extract:

**(a) Scalar α (zeroth order):** The variance ratio of the original definition, computed from $\hat{H}$:

$$\alpha_0 = \frac{\text{Var}_Y[\hat{H}(Y)]}{\text{Var}[\theta_{\text{obs}, t+\Delta t}]}$$

This recovers the current measurement as a special case.

**(b) Coupling asymmetry β (first order):** Fit the learned $\hat{H}$ to the ReKu form to extract the asymmetry parameter:

$$\hat{H}(Y) \approx A \cdot \sin(\Delta\phi(Y)) \cdot (1 + \tanh(\beta \cdot \Delta\phi(Y)))$$

The extracted $\beta$ gives the **cascade level directly** — $\beta \approx 0$ is pre-cascade, $\beta \gg 1$ is D3.

**(c) Coupling topology (second order):** The full shape of $\hat{H}$ reveals the coupling geometry — whether it's sinusoidal (Kuramoto, balanced), rectified (WTA, captured), harmonic (oscillating), or Coulombic (long-range). This tells you which **gauge projection** (§58L) the system is in.

**(d) Eckert manifold position:** The triple $(O, R, \alpha_0)$ from current measurement plus $(\beta, \text{topology})$ from the learned $\hat{H}$ gives a **richer coordinate** on the Eckert manifold. The scalar $\alpha$ is the radial component; $\beta$ and topology are the angular components.

**What this changes for Pe scoring:**

| Current (parametric) | Proposed (PINN) |
|---------------------|-----------------|
| $\alpha$ = scalar (variance ratio) | $\hat{H}(Y)$ = full coupling function |
| Assumes linear coupling | Learns arbitrary coupling shape |
| No cascade information in $\alpha$ itself | $\beta$ extracted directly = cascade level |
| All domains use same measurement | Gauge projection identified from coupling topology |
| Requires clean, dense time series | Works with sparse, noisy data (IC-PINN result) |

**Why this matters for credibility:**

The current α measurement is a **summary statistic**. It compresses the coupling function into a single number. This is fine for initial scoring (and matches well — the 20 convergences work with the scalar). But for Paper 131 (Kramers unification across five domains) and for the (3,2) gauge equivalence claim, we need to show that the SHAPE of the coupling function varies across domains in the way predicted by the gauge projections.

The PINN protocol provides this. If you score a social media platform and get $\hat{H}$ ≈ sinusoidal (Gauge A), and score a clinical jailbreak system and get $\hat{H}$ ≈ rectified (Gauge B → Kramers), and both produce the same Pe value but with different coupling topologies connected by an Sp(2,R) transformation — that is a **direct test of gauge equivalence**. The IC-PINN method makes this measurement possible without assuming the answer.

**Practical implementation path:**

1. **Phase 1 (now):** Use existing scored platforms (N=86) with time-series data. Train IC-PINN on each platform's output→user time series. Extract $\hat{H}$, $\alpha_0$, $\beta$ for each.
2. **Phase 2:** Cluster platforms by coupling topology ($\hat{H}$ shape). Check if clusters match the four gauge projections (scoring, Kramers, Coulomb, oscillator).
3. **Phase 3:** For platform pairs in different topology clusters but with similar Pe: check if an Sp(2,R) transformation connects their $\hat{H}$ functions. This is the gauge equivalence test (K-LIFT-6).
4. **Phase 4:** Deploy as standard measurement in the scoring pipeline. Replace scalar $\alpha$ with the full coupling triple $(\alpha_0, \beta, \text{topology})$.

**Kill condition:** If the learned coupling functions $\hat{H}$ across domains are all approximately sinusoidal (standard Kuramoto) with no significant $\beta$ variation, then:
- The gauge projection structure is irrelevant (only one gauge observed)
- The α-timelike argument from coupling asymmetry collapses
- The D3 attractor has no synchronization basin structure — it's just a large-amplitude version of the same sinusoidal coupling

This would not kill Pe itself (the scalar still works), but it would kill the (3,2) interpretation.

**References:**
- Hwang, Jo, Kim, "Data-driven inference of coupling functions in oscillatory systems via physics-informed neural networks," Phys. Rev. Research 8, 013259, 2026.
- Riedel-Kruse, Oates et al., "Nonreciprocal synchronization in embryonic oscillator ensembles," PNAS 121(35), 2024.
- Raissi, Perdikaris, Karniadakis, "Physics-informed neural networks: A deep learning framework for solving forward and inverse problems involving nonlinear partial differential equations," J. Comput. Phys. 378, 2019 (original PINN paper).
